title: Nine-round AES-256 single-key MITM key recovery, fractional-table tradeoff

target.description: Nine-round AES-256, rounds 0 through 8 in the authors' indexing, with the real AES-256 key schedule, a final AddRoundKey, and the reduced cipher's final MixColumns omitted. Section 4.2 inserts one round in the middle of the eight-round construction, as drawn in Figure 6.

setting.key_relation: One unknown secret AES key; the attacker does not select related keys or obtain related-key oracles.
setting.key_population: general secret key; no weak-key restriction reported
setting.plaintext_model: chosen-plaintext structures under the same designated secret key
assumptions: The Section 4.2 extension keeps the eight-round outer key-enumeration structure while adding one round to the middle multiset computation.
Forty byte parameters describe the extended multiset; the source enumerates 2^208 admissible parameter values rather than unrestricted 2^320 values.
Only a 2^-7 fraction of the possible multisets is stored. Replaying the online attack increases chosen-plaintext and reported online-time budgets by a factor 2^7.
The truncated-differential and table-hit analysis uses expected counts and does not specify a numerical final key-recovery probability.

time.note: Section 4.2 multiplies the inherited 2^196 online estimate by 2^7; Table 1 and the abstract report 2^203. This figure is not asserted to include construction of the retained multiset table, whose separate setup time is not given.

data.note: Section 4.2 repeats the 2^113-chosen-plaintext attack a factor 2^7 more often to compensate for retaining only a 2^-7 fraction of the multiset table; the resulting 2^120 appears in Table 1.

memory.note: Only a 2^-7 fraction of the full table of about 2^210 AES blocks is retained; Section 4.2 and Table 1 report the resulting 2^203-block design point.

preprocessing.note: The retained multiset table must be constructed, but Section 4.2 does not give a separate AES-encryption-equivalent setup budget for the 2^-7-fraction table. The reported 2^203 online estimate must not be interpreted as a verified setup-inclusive total.

success.description: The source compensates for a 2^-7 table fraction with 2^7 more online work and data, restoring the expected table-hit scale. It does not report a numerical overall key-recovery probability; the table fraction is not itself that probability.

review.scope: The defining section and table give expected right-pair/table-hit counts, conditional filtering and completion, but no numerical complete-key recovery probability at this retained parameter choice.

evidence.locator: PDF pp.4-5, Section 2.1, conventions and units; pp.15-16, Section 4.2 and Figure 6; p.8, Table 1, nine-round AES-256 MITM row.
evidence.interpretation: The primary construction reduces the 2^210-block full table by a factor 2^7 and explicitly increases both time and data by 2^7. Its resulting 2^203 time, 2^120 chosen-plaintext data and 2^203-block memory agree with its own Table 1. Separate preprocessing and numerical success are not supplied, and no security lower bound follows.

evidence.locator: PDF pp.1–17 complete read; p.5native units; pp.10–13 seven-round costs and completion; pp.14–16 schedule-dependent extensions.
evidence.interpretation: Raw-first independent full inventory, original-PDF SHA recheck, bounded official version/successor checks. Existing quoted resource tuple and stableIDpreserved; no author code executed.

evidence.locator: PDF7 Section2 fractional-table success condition; PDF15–16 Section4.2, full table and 2^-7 fractional-table repetition.
evidence.interpretation: Targeted success audit: expected counts and conditional correctness are retained without inventing an end-to-end probability or a Poisson independence assumption.

limitations: The attack and extended multiset enumeration have not been independently implemented or reproduced.
The reported time does not establish an end-to-end bound including table generation; preprocessing remains null rather than zero.
The source's expected-hit argument does not provide a numerical final success probability or justify automatic frontier comparison.
This record preserves the inspected 2013 source version and is not a claim of current best-known cryptanalysis.
